findings.title: Negative-offset "advanced pagination" branch is fundamentally broken with Django querysets
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly disallows negative slice indices and raises an exception (`Negative indexing is not supported.`) rather than handling it the way list slicing would. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is incorrect. As soon as this code path is reached (any authorized user supplies a cursor string with a negative offset while `enable_advanced_features=True`), the request will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of paginated results, making the entire 'advanced pagination' feature non-functional and a self-inflicted DoS vector for whoever can trigger it.

findings.title: Overly broad authorization gate for a pagination path that crashes
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` allows any organization member with "global access" (not just superusers/admins) to opt into `OptimizedCursorPaginator` via the `optimized_pagination=true` query param. The in-code comments describe this as being for "authorized administrators" only, but `has_global_access` is a much weaker bar than superuser. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling in `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (see paginator.py finding), this means a relatively large set of non-admin users can trigger unhandled 500s on this endpoint just by crafting a cursor string, and the intended admin-only restriction is not actually enforced as described.

findings.title: Negative-offset clamp only applied for forward pagination, not for prev-cursors
findings.body: In `BasePaginator.get_result`, the new code clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. This only guards the forward-pagination case; when `cursor.is_prev` is True, the raw (potentially negative, since `Cursor.offset` is parsed directly from user-supplied cursor strings via `int(bits[1])`) offset is passed straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which will raise an exception on Django querysets. The fix is incomplete/inconsistent: it protects one pagination direction but leaves the other exposed to the same crash.

findings.title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregate, corrupting timestamp scores on overlapping members
findings.body: After switching the span buffer from Redis sets (`sadd`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zunionstore`) keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, the `zunionstore` calls at lines 47 and 53 do not specify `AGGREGATE MIN`, so Redis defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same member (identical span payload) exists in both sets being merged — e.g. in the edge case where `parent_span_id == span_id` causes `span_key` to equal `set_key`, or if a span payload is present under more than one bucket due to redirect processing/retries — its score (meant to represent an end timestamp used for both flush-timeout tracking and the new `zpopmin` eviction) gets summed with itself, producing a corrupted, non-timestamp value. This can cause spans to be evicted/retained in the wrong order or to never expire as intended, silently defeating the new eviction logic this PR introduces.

findings.title: Redirect-depth safety limit cut 10x without justification or test coverage
findings.body: The loop bound for resolving the redirect chain was reduced from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the previous explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed entirely rather than updated. This silently lowers the maximum depth of a redirect/parent chain that can be correctly resolved before the script gives up, risking incorrect segment joining for deeply-nested span trees that previously worked. No test exercises this changed limit, and the change is unrelated to and undocumented in the PR description, which only discusses buffer eviction.

findings.title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code, and its prior observability was removed without replacement
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but after this change nothing in `buffer.py` reads `self.max_segment_spans` anymore. Previously, `_load_segment_data` used this value to detect and skip (with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log) segments whose span count exceeded the limit. That enforcement and its metric were removed in favor of the Lua script's hard-coded eviction at `span_count > 1000`, but no equivalent metric/log was added for the new eviction path, and the now-unused constructor parameter is misleading to callers/tests who may still pass it expecting enforcement.

findings.title: Eviction cap hardcoded to 1000, decoupled from the Python-configurable (and now-unused) max_segment_spans=1001
findings.body: The eviction threshold `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` is a magic number baked into the Lua script, no longer driven by the `max_segment_spans` setting on `SpansBuffer` (which is unused after this change, see buffer.py finding). The two numbers (1000 here vs. 1001 previously configured in Python) are also off-by-one from each other, making it easy for future maintainers to believe changing `max_segment_spans` has any effect, when it no longer does.

findings.title: New hard-required field `end_timestamp_precise` with no fallback risks consumer crash on rollout/old messages
findings.body: `process_batch` now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` using direct dict indexing (unlike the optional `val.get("parent_span_id")` pattern used elsewhere). If any in-flight or backlog Kafka message lacks this field (e.g. during a mixed-version rollout where Relay/producers haven't yet guaranteed this field, or on topic replay of older messages), this raises a `KeyError` that is not handled anywhere in this path, which will fail the whole batch and likely crash/stall the consumer. This is a behavior change from the previous code which did not require this key at all.

findings.title: No test coverage for the new >1000-span eviction behavior added by this PR
findings.body: The PR's stated purpose is "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert," implemented via `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua when a segment's sorted set exceeds 1000 members. None of the changes in this test file add a case that inserts more than 1000 spans into a single segment to verify that the oldest entries are correctly evicted, that the retained spans are the newest ones, or that `flush_segments` behaves correctly afterward. The only changes here are adding the new required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing unrelated test spans, so the core new behavior of this PR is entirely untested.

findings.title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit log endpoint's optimized_pagination flag have no tests
findings.body: This PR adds a new paginator class (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`) with a security-relevant negative-offset code path, and wires it into `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` behind a new query parameter and an authorization check. No tests were added for either the paginator class or the new endpoint branch (e.g. verifying authorized vs. unauthorized access, or correct/incorrect handling of negative offsets). Given the broken negative-offset handling identified separately, tests would have caught this before merge.

findings.title: Misleading comment implies a functional change that doesn't exist in this file
findings.body: The added comment states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios... This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets," but the code on the next line (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — `int()` already accepted negative numbers. No validation or enablement logic was added here. The comment is misleading: it suggests this file deliberately sanctions negative offsets as a safe, supported feature, while the actual consumers of `Cursor.offset` (in paginator.py) do not safely support negative values and will raise exceptions when given one. This can mislead future maintainers into believing negative offsets are a vetted, working feature.

findings.title: Unrelated, security-sensitive pagination feature bundled into a PR described as a spans-buffer optimization
findings.body: This PR's title/description describe an optimization to the spans Redis buffer (add-buffer.lua, buffer.py), but it also introduces and wires up an entirely new, broken pagination mechanism (`OptimizedCursorPaginator`, negative-offset cursor handling, and a new `optimized_pagination` endpoint flag in the audit log API) that is unrelated to spans buffering. This combination of an unrelated, under-tested, and crash-prone authorization-adjacent feature with a narrowly-described infra change is the kind of change that should be split into its own PR with explicit review of its authorization model and failure modes; as bundled, it is easy for reviewers focused on the stated spans-buffer change to miss the new attack surface in the pagination code.
